it handles the mixing period correctly while keeping $X$ fixed at the assumed
value, so the `flag0`–`forward` gap isolates what the mixing treatment
contributes beyond the reporting-rate channel. Experiment C is the experiment
that overturns the other Experiment B headlines, so the decomposition should not
be assumed to carry over.

```{r}
#| label: exp-c-gap
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-cap: "Median bias for flag0 and forward in Experiment C. The vertical distance between the two series is the contribution of the deterministic mixing treatment, holding the reporting-rate treatment fixed."
ggplot(summ_c[mode %in% c("flag0", "forward")],
       aes(factor(100 * trip_pct), med, colour = mode, group = mode)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  facet_grid(X_assumed ~ phi,
             labeller = labeller(phi = function(x) paste0("phi = ", x),
                                 X_assumed = function(x) paste0("X = ", x))) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal) +
  labs(x = "Trip size (% of release group)", y = "Median relative bias in F-hat",
       colour = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| label: exp-c-gap-inline
#| include: false
gap_safe <- c_gap[X_assumed == 0.50 & phi == 1, max(abs(gap))]
gap_bad  <- c_gap[X_assumed == 0.20 & phi == 2, range(gap)]
gap_max  <- c_gap[which.max(abs(gap))]
```

Note that in this experiment the reporting rate is correct on average, so
`forward` is not carrying a reporting-rate error in the way it does in
Experiments A and B; the gap here isolates the deterministic inversion against a
correctly specified alternative rather than decomposing a misspecification. Where
the floor is inactive ($X_{assumed} = 0.5$, $\varphi = 1$) the two agree to
within `r fpc(gap_safe, 0, signed = FALSE)`. Where it is active the gap widens to
`r fpc_range(gap_bad)`, with the largest single gap
(`r fpc(gap_max$gap)`) at $X_{assumed} = `r gap_max$X_assumed`$,
$\varphi = `r gap_max$phi`$, trip size `r 100 * gap_max$trip_pct`%. The
deterministic treatment is therefore a second-order channel exactly where the
floor is inactive and a first-order one where it is not — the same boundary that
governs everything else in this experiment.

# Experiment D: the mixing-period recapture fraction

Experiment B varied $\varphi$ and `nmix` separately, which is how an analyst
encounters them — one is a property of the fishery, the other a configuration
choice. But for `flag1` they are not two effects. Both act only by changing how
many tags are recaptured while the mixing rule is in force.

Define

$$\psi = \frac{1}{N_0}\sum_{t \le n_{mix}} C_t,$$

the expected fraction of a release group recaptured during the mixing period.
This is directly computable from a real `.tag` file given `tag_flags(i,1)`,
which makes it the useful axis: an analyst can measure $\psi$ for their own data
and read off the expected bias.

## Why $\psi$ should govern the `flag1` bias {#sec-why-psi}

`flag1` removes $R_t$ where it should remove $C_t$, so in expectation it
under-removes by $(1 - X)\,C_t$ each mixing period, and $(1-X)\,\psi N_0$ in
total. The surviving tagged cohort entering the informative periods is therefore
too large by that amount. Predicted recaptures scale with the cohort, so to
match the observed post-mixing returns the model compensates with a smaller $F$:

$$\frac{\hat{F}}{F} \;\approx\; \frac{N_{post}}{N_{post} + (1-X)\,\psi N_0},
\qquad N_{post} = N_0\,e^{-(\varphi F + M)\,n_{mix}}.$$

Note carefully what this does and does not predict. The bias depends on
$\varphi$ and `nmix` only through $\psi$ and $N_{post}$ — but $N_{post}$ carries
an `nmix` dependence of its own, over and above the one that runs through
$\psi$. Two configurations with different $\varphi$ and `nmix` but the same
$\psi$ are therefore predicted to be *close*, not identical, and the one with
the longer mixing period is predicted to be the worse of the two: it reaches
the same recapture fraction with a smaller surviving cohort to carry the
un-removed tags. Whether that separation is large enough to matter for an
assessment is a quantitative question, and it is the one the sufficiency test
below is built to answer.

```{r}
#| label: exp-d-setup
psi_of <- function(p, phi, nmix) {
  n <- p$N0; tot <- 0
  for (t in seq_len(nmix)) {
    tot <- tot + baranov(p$F_true * phi, n, p$M)
    n   <- n * exp(-(p$F_true * phi + p$M))
  }
  tot / p$N0
}

bias_pred <- function(p, phi, nmix, X) {
  psi   <- psi_of(p, phi, nmix)
  npost <- p$N0 * exp(-(p$F_true * phi + p$M) * nmix)
  under <- (1 - X) * psi * p$N0
  -under / (npost + under)
}

# psi_of() is monotone increasing in phi at fixed nmix, so it can be inverted
# for a target recapture fraction. This is what turns psi from an outcome of
# the design into a controlled variable, and it is the whole basis of the
# sufficiency test below: without it, no two cells share a psi exactly.
phi_for_psi <- function(target, nmix, p = om, phi_max = 20) {
  if (psi_of(p, phi_max, nmix) < target) return(NA_real_)
  uniroot(function(ph) psi_of(p, ph, nmix) - target,
          interval = c(1e-8, phi_max), tol = 1e-10)$root
}

# The loop in psi_of() and the closed form below are the same quantity: summing
# Baranov catch over a geometrically declining cohort telescopes to
# (phi*F/Z)(1 - exp(-nmix*Z)). Asserting it keeps the two from drifting if
# either is edited, and documents where the closed form comes from -- it is the
# expression an analyst needs to compute expected psi for a configuration they
# have not run.
psi_closed <- function(p, phi, nmix) {
  z <- p$F_true * phi + p$M
  (p$F_true * phi / z) * (1 - exp(-nmix * z))
}
stopifnot(all(abs(mapply(function(ph, nm) psi_of(om, ph, nm) -
                           psi_closed(om, ph, nm),
                         c(0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 3),
                         c(2L, 3L, 4L, 2L, 3L))) < 1e-12))
```

## Simulation

Reporting is left un-clumped here so that $\psi$ is isolated from the dispersion
effects of Experiment C. Four release groups of 2,000 tags, correct reporting
rate throughout, so the *only* thing varying is how much of each group is
recaptured before the mixing rule releases its grip.

```{r}
#| label: exp-d-run
n_rep_d <- 40
N0_d    <- 2000
G_d     <- 4

design_d <- CJ(phi  = c(0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0),
               nmix = c(2L, 3L, 4L),
               mode = c("flag0", "flag1"),
               rep  = seq_len(n_rep_d), sorted = FALSE)
design_d[, cell := .GRP, by = .(phi, nmix)]

res_d <- design_d[, {
  set.seed(1000L * cell + rep)
  gs <- lapply(seq_len(G_d), function(g)
    list(N0 = N0_d,
         returns = simulate_group(om, N0_d, om$X_assumed, phi, nmix,
                                  trip_size = 1, stochastic = TRUE)))
  fit_multi(gs, om, mode = mode, nmix = nmix)
}, by = .(rep, cell, phi, nmix, mode)]

res_d[, `:=`(mode = factor(mode, levels = c("flag0", "flag1")),
             rel_bias = F_hat / om$F_true - 1)]

summ_d <- res_d[conv == 0, .(bias = median(rel_bias),
                             mcse = mcse_median(F_hat) / om$F_true),
                by = .(phi, nmix, mode)]
summ_d[, psi  := psi_of(om, phi, nmix), by = .(phi, nmix)]
summ_d[, pred := bias_pred(om, phi, nmix, om$X_assumed), by = .(phi, nmix)]
```

```{r}
#| label: exp-d-plot
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "Median relative bias against the mixing-period recapture fraction. Points are simulated, with error bars at two Monte Carlo standard errors; the dashed line is the analytic prediction for flag1. Configurations with different phi and nmix collapse onto a single curve."
ggplot(summ_d, aes(psi, bias)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(data = summ_d[mode == "flag1"][order(psi)],
            aes(y = pred), linetype = 2, colour = "grey30") +
  geom_linerange(aes(ymin = bias - 2 * mcse, ymax = bias + 2 * mcse,
                     colour = mode), alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = mode, shape = factor(nmix)), size = 2.4) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal) +
  labs(x = expression(psi~"(fraction of release group recaptured during mixing)"),
       y = "Median relative bias in F-hat",
       colour = NULL, shape = "nmix")
```

```{r}
#| label: exp-d-table
tab_d <- merge(dcast(summ_d, phi + nmix + psi ~ mode, value.var = "bias"),
               summ_d[mode == "flag1", .(phi, nmix, predicted = pred)],
               by = c("phi", "nmix"))

knitr::kable(tab_d[order(psi), .(phi, nmix, psi, flag0, flag1, predicted)],
             digits = 3,
             col.names = c("phi", "nmix", "psi", "flag0", "flag1",
                           "flag1 predicted"),
             caption = paste0(
               "Bias against the mixing-period recapture fraction, with the ",
               "analytic prediction."))
```

```{r}
#| label: exp-d-check
d_cor <- summ_d[mode == "flag1", cor(bias, pred)]
cat(sprintf("Correlation between simulated and predicted flag1 bias: %.4f\n",
            d_cor))
```

```{r}
#| label: exp-d-inline
#| include: false
d_f0 <- summ_d[mode == "flag0"]
d_f0_max <- d_f0[which.max(abs(bias))]
d_f0_sig <- d_f0[abs(bias) > 2 * mcse]
```

## Is $\psi$ sufficient?

The design above crosses $\varphi$ and `nmix` and reports whatever $\psi$ falls
out, so no two cells share a $\psi$ exactly and the collapse onto a single curve
can only be judged by eye against the fitted line. The question the prediction
actually raises — whether two configurations with the *same* $\psi$ behave the
same — needs a design in which $\psi$ is controlled rather than observed.

Inverting `psi_of()` supplies one. Solving for the $\varphi$ that delivers a
target $\psi$ at each mixing length puts the cells on a common $\psi$ grid, and
fitting to expected rather than simulated returns removes the Monte Carlo noise
entirely, so any separation between mixing lengths at the same $\psi$ is
structural rather than scatter. No Monte Carlo standard errors are reported in
this subsection because there is no Monte Carlo.

```{r}
#| label: exp-d-suff-calib
PSI_TARGETS <- c(0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.40, 0.50)

calib <- CJ(psi_t = PSI_TARGETS, nmix = 2:4)
calib[, phi := mapply(phi_for_psi, psi_t, nmix)]
calib <- calib[is.finite(phi)]

knitr::kable(dcast(calib, psi_t ~ nmix, value.var = "phi"), digits = 2,
             col.names = c("psi", "nmix = 2", "nmix = 3", "nmix = 4"),
             caption = paste0(
               "Availability multiplier required to reach each target ",
               "recapture fraction, by mixing length."))
```

This calibration table is worth reading before the results. Reaching a high
$\psi$ over a short mixing period requires a large availability multiplier;
reaching the same $\psi$ over four periods requires much less. The top two rows
need multipliers above the range Experiment B covered, so they complete the grid
rather than describing configurations anyone should expect to meet.

```{r}
#| label: exp-d-suff
grid_suff <- CJ(psi_t = PSI_TARGETS, nmix = 2:4,
                mode = c("flag0", "flag1"), sorted = FALSE)
grid_suff <- merge(grid_suff, calib, by = c("psi_t", "nmix"))

res_suff <- grid_suff[, {
  # One release group, expected returns, correct reporting rate. The Poisson
  # kernel rather than dpois(), because expected returns are not integers.
  g <- list(list(N0      = om$N0,
                 returns = simulate_group(om, om$N0, om$X_assumed, phi, nmix,
                                          trip_size = 1, stochastic = FALSE,
                                          expected = TRUE)))
  cbind(fit_multi(g, om, mode = mode, nmix = nmix, kernel = TRUE),
        floored = floor_check(g, om, nmix)$any)
}, by = .(psi_t, nmix, phi, mode)]

res_suff[, `:=`(rel_bias = F_hat / om$F_true - 1,
                psi      = mapply(function(ph, nm) psi_of(om, ph, nm),
                                  phi, nmix))]
res_suff[, pred := mapply(function(ph, nm) bias_pred(om, ph, nm, om$X_assumed),
                          phi, nmix)]

# The inversion should be exact, and nothing here should be sitting on a search
# bound or against the survival floor -- if either happens the numbers below
# describe the machinery rather than the estimator.
stopifnot(max(abs(res_suff$psi - res_suff$psi_t)) < 1e-8,
          !any(res_suff$at_bound))
```

```{r}
#| label: exp-d-suff-table
suff_f1 <- res_suff[mode == "flag1"]
suff_f0 <- res_suff[mode == "flag0"]

knitr::kable(dcast(suff_f1, psi_t ~ nmix, value.var = "rel_bias"), digits = 3,
             col.names = c("psi", "nmix = 2", "nmix = 3", "nmix = 4"),
             caption = paste0(
               "Structural relative bias in F-hat under tag_flags(i,2) = 1, ",
               "at a controlled recapture fraction (rows) and mixing length ",
               "(columns), with the reporting rate correctly specified at ",
               fnum(om$X_assumed, 2), ". Monte Carlo noise is absent by ",
               "construction."))
```

```{r}
#| label: exp-d-suff-inline
#| include: false
suff_sp <- suff_f1[, .(best   = max(rel_bias),          # least negative
                       worst  = min(rel_bias),          # most negative
                       spread = max(rel_bias) - min(rel_bias)),
                   by = psi_t][order(psi_t)]

# Is the ordering the theory predicts -- longer mixing worse at the same psi --
# present at every target?
suff_mono <- suff_f1[order(nmix), .(mono = all(diff(rel_bias) < 0)),
                     by = psi_t][, all(mono)]

suff_top     <- suff_sp[which.max(psi_t)]
suff_top_psi <- max(suff_sp$psi_t)
suff_at      <- function(p) suff_sp[abs(psi_t - p) < 1e-9]

# How much of the separation does the analytic predictor account for? It carries
# the same nmix dependence through N_post, so it should reproduce the ordering;
# the interesting question is whether it gets the size right.
suff_pred_sp <- suff_f1[, .(spread = max(pred) - min(pred)), by = psi_t
                        ][which.max(psi_t), spread]

suff_f0_max <- suff_f0[which.max(abs(rel_bias))]

# TRIPWIRE. The ordering claim -- that a longer mixing period carries a worse
# bias than a short one at the same psi -- is asserted in the results and
# guidance sections, and the executive summary quotes bias magnitudes against
# psi before this chunk runs. Neither can be an inline expression at the point
# of use, so both are guarded here: if the ordering ever reverses, or the
# separation at the top of the grid collapses to something an assessment could
# ignore, the render fails rather than shipping prose that contradicts the
# results. The margin is deliberately generous -- this is a structural
# prediction, not a marginal one -- so a trip means something real changed, not
# that the design drifted. Update the prose and this guard together.
SUFF_MIN_SPREAD <- 0.02

# The summary also states, before this chunk runs, that the bias reaches half of
# F or more by psi = 0.5. The guard is set at exactly that mark rather than
# below it: a guard at 0.48 would pass at 0.485, which is a value the summary's
# wording does not describe, and a guard that admits states the prose gets wrong
# is not guarding the prose. The margin is thin -- the shortest mixing length
# clears half by well under a percentage point -- but the quantity is
# deterministic, so it will not drift on a tolerance change. A trip means the
# operating model or the grid moved, which is a reason to reread the summary
# rather than a reason to loosen the guard.
SUFF_MIN_TOP <- 0.50

stopifnot(suff_mono,
          suff_top$spread > SUFF_MIN_SPREAD,
          abs(suff_top$best) > SUFF_MIN_TOP)

# Reported whether or not the guard trips, so a trip is immediately diagnosable.
message(sprintf(paste0(
  "Experiment D sufficiency: monotone = %s; at psi = %.2f the spread is ",
  "%.4f (guard %.2f) and the smallest bias is %.4f (guard %.2f)"),
  suff_mono, suff_top_psi, suff_top$spread, SUFF_MIN_SPREAD,
  abs(suff_top$best), SUFF_MIN_TOP))
```

$\psi$ is close to sufficient, but it is not sufficient. At every target the
ordering the theory predicts is present — a longer mixing period carries the
worse bias at the same recapture fraction — and the separation widens as $\psi$
does, from `r fpc(suff_at(min(PSI_TARGETS))$spread, 1, signed = FALSE)` at
$\psi = `r fnum(min(PSI_TARGETS), 2)`$ to
`r fpc(suff_top$spread, 1, signed = FALSE)` at
$\psi = `r fnum(suff_top_psi, 2)`$. Against a bias of
`r fpc(suff_top$worst, 1)` in that worst cell, a spread of that size is second
order but not negligible: an analyst reading a single number off a $\psi$ curve
is making an error of roughly
`r fpc(suff_top$spread / abs(suff_top$worst), 0, signed = FALSE)` of the
quantity they are estimating, in a known direction.

That the separation exists is not a failure of the theory in
@sec-why-psi — the predictor carries the same `nmix` dependence through
$N_{post}$ and reproduces the ordering, giving a spread of
`r fpc(suff_pred_sp, 1, signed = FALSE)` at the top of the grid against the
fitted `r fpc(suff_top$spread, 1, signed = FALSE)`. The approximation
`r if (suff_pred_sp > suff_top$spread) "overstates" else "understates"` the
effect while getting its sign and ordering right. What fails is the looser
statement, easy to make from the fitted curve alone, that the bias is a
function of $\psi$ *simpliciter*. It is a function of $\psi$ and the mixing length, with the
second term small.

`flag0` is flat across the whole grid, as it must be: with expected returns and
a correct reporting rate its inversion is exact. Its largest absolute deviation
anywhere in the design is `r fpc(abs(suff_f0_max$rel_bias), 4, signed = FALSE)`,
which is the optimiser's tolerance rather than a property of the estimator, and
it is worth contrasting with the `r fpc(abs(d_f0_max$bias), 1, signed = FALSE)`
residual in the Monte Carlo design above: that residual is sampling scatter, not
structure, and this is the run that demonstrates it.
`r if (any(res_suff$floored)) "Note that the survival floor engaged in at least one cell, so the flag0 benchmark in those cells is not clean." else "The survival floor did not engage anywhere in this design, so the flag0 row is a clean benchmark and the flag1 numbers are attributable to the mixing-period treatment alone."`

## Reading this for a real assessment

The near-collapse onto a single curve is the practical result. `flag1`'s bias is
not a property of the mixing-period length or of tag availability separately — it
is largely a function of the recapture fraction those two things produce, and
that fraction is measurable. For a real release group:

1. Take `tag_flags(i,1)` for that group and sum the *reported returns* within
   that many periods of release.
2. Raise by the assumed reporting rate and divide by the number released:
   $\hat\psi_i \approx (1/X)\sum_{t \le \texttt{tag\_flags}(i,1)} R_{it} / N_i$.
   The `.tag` file records returns, not recaptures, so omitting the $1/X$
   returns $X\psi$ — at a reporting rate near 0.5, half the true fraction.
3. Read the expected downward bias in $F$ off the curve, or evaluate
   $-(1-X)\psi N_0 / (N_{post} + (1-X)\psi N_0)$ directly. Where the mixing
   period is long, take the pessimistic end of the range at that $\psi$.

Two caveats travel with $\hat\psi$. The raising uses the same assumed reporting
rate whose correctness is in question, so $\hat\psi$ inherits that error — and
inherits it in the unhelpful direction, since a reporting rate that is too high
understates $\psi$ and therefore understates the bias. And a
release-group-weighted mean aggregates over groups whose mixing lengths and
availabilities differ, whereas the figures here apply a single value to a single
cohort.

At $\psi = 0.05$ the bias is
`r fpc_range(unlist(suff_at(0.05)[, .(worst, best)]), 1)` and arguably
tolerable. By $\psi = 0.3$ it is
`r fpc_range(unlist(suff_at(0.30)[, .(worst, best)]), 1)`, and by
$\psi = `r fnum(suff_top_psi, 2)`$ it reaches
`r fpc_range(unlist(suff_top[, .(worst, best)]), 1)`.
Whether `tag_flags(i,2) = 1` is defensible for a given assessment is therefore
an empirical question about that assessment's tag data, not a general one — and
it is a question the assessment team can answer in an afternoon.

`flag0` is far flatter across the same range, but it is not exactly zero: its
largest absolute median bias is `r fpc(d_f0_max$bias)` at $\psi =
`r fnum(d_f0_max$psi, 2)`$, and `r nrow(d_f0_sig)` of the `r nrow(d_f0)` cells
`r if (nrow(d_f0_sig) == 1) "sits" else "sit"` more than two Monte Carlo
standard errors from zero.
`r if (!nrow(d_f0_sig)) "No cell is individually distinguishable from zero." else if (nrow(d_f0_sig) == 1L) paste0("That single exception carries a ", if (d_f0_sig$bias > 0) "positive" else "negative", " sign and ", if (d_f0_sig$psi > median(d_f0$psi)) "sits at the high-$\\psi$ end of the design" else "sits in the body of the design", ".") else paste0("The exceptions carry a ", if (all(d_f0_sig$bias > 0)) "positive" else if (all(d_f0_sig$bias < 0)) "negative" else "mixed", " sign and ", if (min(d_f0_sig$psi) > median(d_f0$psi)) "sit at the high-$\\psi$ end of the design" else "are scattered across the design", ".")`
Whether that residual is Monte Carlo scatter or a real small-sample property of
inverting a noisy target is what Experiment E asks. Note the direction the
theory predicts: inverting a noisy target is *convex* in the target, so the
mechanism, if present, biases $F$ **upward** at small samples.

# Experiment E: release-group size and the noisy-inversion bias

The `flag0` residuals at high $\psi$ have a candidate explanation. The estimator
inverts an *observed* quantity: it solves for the $F$ that removes
$R_t / X_{assumed}$ tags. That inversion is a convex function of the target over
the relevant range, so by Jensen's inequality the expectation of the solved $F$
exceeds the $F$ that would be solved from the expected target. The size of the
gap grows with the noise-to-signal ratio of $R_t$, which falls with
release-group size.

If that is the mechanism, `flag0`'s bias should decline systematically as $N_0$
rises, holding $\psi$ fixed. It would matter if it did: it would be a *third*
condition on the default's unbiasedness — adequate release-group size —
independent of both the reporting rate and the survival floor, and small release
groups are the realistic case once releases are split by region and quarter.

Three design points are worth stating before the result, because each of them
determines whether the experiment can detect the effect it is looking for and
whether the number it reports means what it appears to mean.

**The statistic has to be tail-aware, and the mean alone is not enough.**
Jensen's inequality is a statement about $E[\hat{F}]$, so the median — close to
invariant under the monotone convexity being hypothesised — tests the mechanism
with an instrument largely blind to it. But the mean has a problem of its own
here. The solved $F$ is unbounded above in principle and bounded in practice
only by the search interval, so if the effect is carried by a handful of extreme
replicates, the mean is partly a report on where the interval was placed. Three
statistics are therefore reported together: the **frequency of gross overshoot**
(the proportion of replicates returning $\hat{F}$ more than
`r E_TAIL_MULT`$\times$ the truth), which is the primary statistic because it is
a bounded frequency and insensitive to the interval as long as the ceiling sits
well above the threshold; the mean, which is what the convexity argument speaks
to; and the median, for comparability with the rest of this document.

**The whole design is run at two search intervals.** Every cell is fitted twice,
once over the interval used everywhere else in this document and once over a
much wider one. If the reported effect is a property of the estimator, the two
runs agree. If it is a property of the ceiling, they do not, and the mean is
then not a quantity worth quoting. This check is reported before the verdict,
not after it.

**One release group, not four.** `fit_multi` pools groups into a single
objective, so four groups over four mixing periods averages sixteen independent
noisy inversions before $\hat{F}$ is formed. That averaging is exactly what the
large-sample argument says washes the bias out, so pooling suppresses the
quantity of interest. Experiment E therefore uses a single group, which
maximises the noise-to-signal ratio available at a given $N_0$.

Recapture fraction is held high — $\psi = `r fnum(psi_of(om, 2.0, 4L), 2)`$,
toward the upper end of the Experiment D range — because that is where the
Experiment D residuals appeared. Total tags vary with group size, which affects
the precision of the estimates but not their expectation; the MCSE columns are
what to read against.

Runtime note: fitting at two intervals doubles this design, and the replicate
count is set high because a tail frequency needs more replicates than a mean
does. Every fit is still one-dimensional, so this remains among the cheaper of
the five experiments; drop `n_rep_e` for a quick pass, but check the guard
margin reported at the end of the section before trusting the verdict.

```{r}
#| label: exp-e-run
# A tail frequency is a much lower-powered statistic than a mean, so this
# experiment needs more replicates than a median-based one would. At the tail
# mass seen here, 200 replicates leaves the difference between the smallest and
# largest group sizes barely separable from its own Monte Carlo error.
n_rep_e <- 400
PHI_E   <- 2.0
NMIX_E  <- 4L
G_e     <- 1          # one group: pooling averages away the effect being tested

# The same simulated data are fitted over both intervals, so the two runs are
# paired and any difference is attributable to the ceiling alone.
intervals_e <- list(default = LOGF_INT, wide = LOGF_INT_WIDE)

design_e <- CJ(N0_e     = c(125, 250, 500, 2000, 10000),
               interval = names(intervals_e),
               rep      = seq_len(n_rep_e), sorted = FALSE)
design_e[, cell := .GRP, by = .(N0_e)]

res_e <- design_e[, {
  set.seed(1000L * cell + rep)
  gs <- lapply(seq_len(G_e), function(g)
    list(N0 = N0_e,
         returns = simulate_group(om, N0_e, om$X_assumed, PHI_E, NMIX_E,
                                  trip_size = 1, stochastic = TRUE)))
  fit_multi(gs, om, mode = "flag0", nmix = NMIX_E,
            interval = intervals_e[[interval]])
}, by = .(rep, cell, N0_e, interval)]

res_e[, `:=`(rel_bias = F_hat / om$F_true - 1,
             interval = factor(interval, levels = c("default", "wide")))]

# Summary statistics, in the order they should be read: a bounded tail
# frequency first, then the mean the Jensen argument speaks to, then the
# median for comparability, then the diagnostic that says whether the mean can
# be taken at face value.
summarise_e <- function(d) {
  d[, .(tail_frac = mean(F_hat > E_TAIL_MULT * om$F_true),
        tail_mcse = sqrt(mean(F_hat > E_TAIL_MULT * om$F_true) *
                         (1 - mean(F_hat > E_TAIL_MULT * om$F_true)) / .N),
        mean_bias = mean(F_hat) / om$F_true - 1,
        mean_mcse = stats::sd(F_hat) / sqrt(.N) / om$F_true,
        bias      = median(rel_bias),
        mcse      = mcse_median(F_hat) / om$F_true,
        bound_pct = 100 * mean(at_bound),
        n         = .N), by = .(N0_e)][order(N0_e)]
}

summ_e      <- summarise_e(res_e[interval == "default"])
summ_e_wide <- summarise_e(res_e[interval == "wide"])

knitr::kable(
  summ_e[, .(N0_e, tail_frac, tail_mcse, mean_bias, mean_mcse,
             bias, mcse, bound_pct, n)],
  digits = 4,
  col.names = c("Tags per group", paste0("P(F-hat > ", E_TAIL_MULT, "x truth)"),
                "MCSE (tail)", "Mean rel. bias", "MCSE (mean)",
                "Median rel. bias", "MCSE (median)", "% at bound", "n"),
  caption = paste0("flag0 against release-group size, at psi = ",
                   round(psi_of(om, PHI_E, NMIX_E), 3),
                   " (phi = ", PHI_E, ", nmix = ", NMIX_E,
                   ", one release group), over the default search interval."))
```

The final two columns are the ones to read first. `% at bound` is the proportion
of replicates whose estimate is sitting on an endpoint of the search interval;
where it is non-zero, the mean in that row is partly a statement about where the
endpoint was put. The comparison against the wider interval below is what
settles whether it matters.

```{r}
#| label: exp-e-stability
stab_e <- merge(
  summ_e[,      .(N0_e, tail_d = tail_frac, mean_d = mean_bias,
                  med_d = bias, bound_d = bound_pct, mcse_d = mean_mcse)],
  summ_e_wide[, .(N0_e, tail_w = tail_frac, mean_w = mean_bias,
                  med_w = bias, bound_w = bound_pct, mcse_w = mean_mcse)],
  by = "N0_e")

knitr::kable(
  stab_e[, .(N0_e, tail_d, tail_w, mean_d, mean_w, med_d, med_w,
             bound_d, bound_w)],
  digits = 4,
  col.names = c("Tags per group", "Tail (default)", "Tail (wide)",
                "Mean (default)", "Mean (wide)", "Median (default)",
                "Median (wide)", "% bound (default)", "% bound (wide)"),
  caption = paste0("The same design fitted over the default search interval ",
                   "and over a much wider one. Statistics that move between ",
                   "the two columns are properties of the ceiling rather than ",
                   "of the estimator."))
```

```{r}
#| label: exp-e-stability-inline
#| include: false
e_bound_any    <- summ_e[, max(bound_pct)]
e_bound_small  <- summ_e[which.min(N0_e), bound_pct]

# Does the mean survive widening the interval? Compare at the smallest group
# size, which is where the effect lives, against the joint MCSE of the two runs.
e_s_d <- stab_e[which.min(N0_e)]
e_mean_shift <- e_s_d$mean_w - e_s_d$mean_d
e_mean_shift_mcse <- sqrt(e_s_d$mcse_d^2 + e_s_d$mcse_w^2)
e_mean_stable <- abs(e_mean_shift) <= 2 * e_mean_shift_mcse

# The tail frequency should be essentially identical across intervals, since
# the threshold sits well below either ceiling.
e_tail_shift <- e_s_d$tail_w - e_s_d$tail_d
```

`r if (e_bound_any == 0) paste0("No replicate in this design returned an estimate on the boundary of the default search interval, at any group size. The mean is therefore not being truncated, and the two interval runs should and do agree.") else paste0("Boundary contact is not negligible: at the smallest group size ", fnum(e_bound_small, 1), "% of replicates return an estimate sitting on an endpoint of the default interval. The mean at that cell is therefore a censored quantity, and the wide-interval column is the one to read.")`
Widening the interval moves the mean at the smallest group size by
`r fpc(e_mean_shift, 1)`, against a joint Monte Carlo standard error of
`r fpc(e_mean_shift_mcse, 1, signed = FALSE)`, so the mean
`r if (e_mean_stable) "is stable to the choice of ceiling" else "is **not** stable to the choice of ceiling and should not be quoted as a bias estimate"`.
The gross-overshoot frequency moves by `r fpc(e_tail_shift, 1)` — as it should,
since the threshold of `r E_TAIL_MULT`$\times$ the truth lies far below either
ceiling — which is why it is the statistic carried into the summary sections.

```{r}
#| label: exp-e-plot
#| fig-height: 6.5
#| fig-cap: "flag0 against release-group size, with two Monte Carlo standard errors and free y scales. The reporting rate is correct and the survival floor is not engaging, so any departure from zero is attributable to release-group size alone. The top panel is the frequency of gross overshoot, which is a bounded proportion and insensitive to the search interval; the mean and median are shown separately below it because the effect appears in the tail frequency and the mean while the median is uninformative about it, which is the signature of a tail effect rather than a shift."
# Three statistics on a shared x axis, free y scales, so the tail frequency is
# not squashed by the scale of the mean. One ggplot rather than a stacked
# layout, to avoid a package dependency the rest of the document does not have.
e_panel <- rbind(
  summ_e[, .(N0_e, stat = paste0("P(F-hat > ", E_TAIL_MULT, "x truth)"),
             val = tail_frac, mcse = tail_mcse)],
  summ_e[, .(N0_e, stat = "Mean relative bias",
             val = mean_bias, mcse = mean_mcse)],
  summ_e[, .(N0_e, stat = "Median relative bias",
             val = bias, mcse = mcse)])

e_panel[, stat := factor(stat, levels = c(
  paste0("P(F-hat > ", E_TAIL_MULT, "x truth)"),
  "Mean relative bias", "Median relative bias"))]

ggplot(e_panel, aes(N0_e, val)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_linerange(aes(ymin = val - 2 * mcse, ymax = val + 2 * mcse),
                 alpha = 0.7, colour = pal[["flag0"]]) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7, colour = pal[["flag0"]]) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2, colour = pal[["flag0"]]) +
  facet_wrap(~ stat, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  # Break at the design points rather than at decade-ish defaults, which label
  # values the design never visits and leave the smallest group on the panel
  # edge.
  scale_x_log10(breaks = sort(unique(e_panel$N0_e)),
                labels = scales::comma,
                expand = expansion(mult = 0.07)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Tags per release group (log scale)", y = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| label: exp-e-inline
#| include: false
e_small <- summ_e[which.min(N0_e)]
e_large <- summ_e[which.max(N0_e)]

# PRIMARY TEST: the gross-overshoot frequency, which is a bounded proportion
# and insensitive to the search ceiling. Two-sided, so that "no effect" and
# "the opposite of the predicted effect" are distinguishable.
e_tail_gap      <- e_small$tail_frac - e_large$tail_frac
e_tail_gap_mcse <- sqrt(e_small$tail_mcse^2 + e_large$tail_mcse^2)
e_resolved      <- abs(e_tail_gap) > 2 * e_tail_gap_mcse
e_direction     <- if (e_tail_gap > 0) "the direction the convexity argument predicts" else
                                       "the opposite direction to the one predicted"

# SECONDARY: the same test on the mean, retained because it is the quantity
# Jensen's inequality speaks to -- but only interpretable if e_mean_stable.
e_gap      <- e_small$mean_bias - e_large$mean_bias
e_gap_mcse <- sqrt(e_small$mean_mcse^2 + e_large$mean_mcse^2)
e_mean_resolved <- abs(e_gap) > 2 * e_gap_mcse

e_trend_tail <- summ_e[, cor(log(N0_e), tail_frac)]
e_trend_mean <- summ_e[, cor(log(N0_e), mean_bias)]
e_trend_med  <- summ_e[, cor(log(N0_e), bias)]

# Smallest tail-frequency difference this design could have resolved.
e_mde <- 2 * e_tail_gap_mcse

# How many replicates does the overshoot frequency at the smallest cell
# correspond to? Quoting the count keeps the reader's sense of scale honest.
e_small_n_tail <- round(e_small$tail_frac * e_small$n)

# Is the median at the smallest group size distinguishable from zero at all?
# At the tail mass this design produces it is not, and quoting it as a bare
# number invites a reader to treat a quantity with an MCSE several times its
# own size as an estimate of central bias. The point being made is that the
# median is blind to the effect, which is stronger stated as a null than as a
# number. Every site that mentions the median uses `e_med_phrase`, so the
# document cannot end up asserting resolution in one section and denying it in
# another. The executive summary states the same thing in words before this
# chunk runs; the guard below fails the render if that ever stops being true.
e_med_resolved <- abs(e_small$bias) > 2 * e_small$mcse
# Two forms of the same statement. The long one carries the figures and is used
# once, at first mention; the short one is used at every later site, because
# five repetitions of the same parenthesis in as many pages reads as though the
# document has lost track of what it has already said. Both branch on the same
# test, so they cannot disagree.
e_med_phrase   <- if (e_med_resolved) {
  paste0("sits at ", fpc(e_small$bias, 1))
} else {
  paste0("is not distinguishable from zero (", fpc(e_small$bias, 1),
         ", against a Monte Carlo standard error of ",
         fpc(e_small$mcse, 1, signed = FALSE), ")")
}
e_med_phrase_short <- if (e_med_resolved) {
  paste0("sits at ", fpc(e_small$bias, 1))
} else {
  "is not distinguishable from zero"
}
```

At `r e_small$N0_e` tags per group, `r fpc(e_small$tail_frac, 1, signed = FALSE)`
of replicates — `r e_small_n_tail` of `r e_small$n` — return an estimate of $F$
more than `r E_TAIL_MULT` times the truth; at
`r format(e_large$N0_e, big.mark = ",")` the figure is
`r fpc(e_large$tail_frac, 1, signed = FALSE)`. The difference is
`r fpc(e_tail_gap, 1)` against a joint Monte Carlo standard error of
`r fpc(e_tail_gap_mcse, 1, signed = FALSE)`, so the two ends of the design are
`r if (e_resolved) "separated by more than two joint standard errors" else "not separated by two joint standard errors"`.
The corresponding difference in the mean is `r fpc(e_gap, 1)` against a joint
standard error of `r fpc(e_gap_mcse, 1, signed = FALSE)`, which
`r if (e_mean_resolved) "is also resolved" else "is not resolved"`
`r if (e_mean_stable) "and, per the interval check above, is not an artefact of the ceiling" else "-- but per the interval check above it moves when the ceiling moves, so it is reported for completeness rather than as a bias estimate"`.

Across the design the correlation with $\log N_0$ is `r fnum(e_trend_tail, 2)`
on the overshoot frequency and `r fnum(e_trend_mean, 2)` on the mean. The median
behaves differently — its correlation is `r fnum(e_trend_med, 2)` — but the
median at the smallest group size `r e_med_phrase`, so it carries no information
about the effect in either direction. **The honest reading is that the median is
blind to this effect, not that it contradicts it.** That is what the mechanism
predicts. A convex inversion applied to a noisier target moves probability mass
into the right tail; it does not shift the bulk of the distribution the same
way, so the centre stays where it was while the mean is dragged upward by the
minority of groups that report many returns during mixing. Any diagnostic that
looks only at the middle of the distribution will see nothing at all, when what
is actually happening is a heavy right tail.

```{r}
#| label: exp-e-verdict
#| include: false
# One verdict string, three branches, so the prose is a single paragraph
# whichever way the result falls.
e_verdict <- if (e_resolved && e_tail_gap > 0) {
  paste0("**The effect is resolved, and it runs in ", e_direction, ".** ",
         "That makes release-group size a third condition on the default's ",
         "unbiasedness, independent of the reporting rate and the survival ",
         "floor: the deterministic inversion is unbiased in the large-sample ",
         "limit, not in general. The form the failure takes is a tail rather ",
         "than a shift -- at ", e_small$N0_e, " tags per group roughly one ",
         "release group in ", fnum(1 / max(e_small$tail_frac, 1e-9), 0),
         " returns an estimate more than ", E_TAIL_MULT, " times the truth, ",
         "while the median at that cell ", e_med_phrase_short, " -- ",
         "so assessments built from many small release groups should not ",
         "expect the Experiment B robustness result to hold at face value, ",
         "and should not expect a median-based diagnostic to warn them.")
} else if (e_resolved) {
  paste0("**The difference is resolved, but it runs in ", e_direction, ".** ",
         "The convexity argument predicts more mass in the upper tail at ",
         "small samples, so this is not confirmation of that mechanism and ",
         "should not be reported as one. Some other small-sample property of ",
         "the inversion is operating, and this design does not identify it.")
} else {
  paste0("**This is an underpowered null, not evidence of absence.** The ",
         "design resolves a difference of about ",
         fpc(e_mde, 1, signed = FALSE), " in overshoot frequency between the ",
         "smallest and largest group sizes, and the convexity effect at these ",
         "sample sizes may well be smaller than that. What can be said is ",
         "that no group-size effect large enough to matter for an assessment ",
         "showed up, and that the Experiment D residuals are consistent with ",
         "Monte Carlo scatter. The mechanism remains plausible on theoretical ",
         "grounds and is not ruled out here.")
}

# The executive summary states a fixed NUMBER of conditions on flag0's
# unbiasedness, and it renders before this chunk runs, so it cannot be an
# inline expression. This is the guard: if Experiment E ever stops resolving an
# upward effect, the render fails here rather than shipping a summary that
# contradicts the results section. Update EXEC_CONDITIONS and the summary
# together.
#
# The guard is tied to the gross-overshoot frequency rather than to the mean,
# because the mean can move with the search interval and a tripwire that can be
# tripped by a change of ceiling is not a tripwire worth having.
EXEC_CONDITIONS <- 3L
stopifnot(
  "Executive summary claims a third condition that Experiment E no longer supports." =
    (EXEC_CONDITIONS == 3L) == (e_resolved && e_tail_gap > 0),
  # The summary also asserts, before this chunk runs, that the median is
  # uninformative about the tail effect. If the median ever becomes
  # distinguishable from zero the summary is wrong, and the results and
  # guidance sections will quote a number the summary has dismissed.
  "Executive summary calls the median uninformative, but it is now resolved." =
    !e_med_resolved)

# Reported whether or not the guard trips, so that a trip is immediately
# diagnosable: a margin below 1 means the design failed to resolve the effect
# and the fix is more replicates, not a rewrite of the executive summary.
message(sprintf(
  "Experiment E guard: tail gap %.4f, joint MCSE %.4f, margin %.2f (needs > 1)",
  e_tail_gap, e_tail_gap_mcse, e_tail_gap / (2 * e_tail_gap_mcse)))

# Follow-on paragraph. If the effect resolved, the interesting fact is that it
# lives in the tail; if it did not, the interesting fact is what would resolve
# it. Either way the extension pointer is the same.
e_lever <- paste0(
  "The obvious lever is the assumed reporting rate: at fixed $N_0$, a lower ",
  "$X_{assumed}$ thins $R_t$ directly and inflates the divisor, attacking ",
  "both sides of the ratio at once. That is listed under ",
  "[Suggested extensions] rather than run here, because the low-$X$ region is ",
  "also where the survival floor engages, and separating the two mechanisms ",
  "needs a design that holds the floor inactive by construction.")

e_next <- if (e_resolved && e_tail_gap > 0) {
  paste0("The three statistics have to be read together, and none of them is ",
         "sufficient alone. At ", e_small$N0_e, " tags per group the median ",
         e_med_phrase_short, ", the mean is ",
         fpc(e_small$mean_bias, 1),
         if (e_mean_stable) "" else
           " (interval-sensitive, and quoted here only for completeness)",
         ", and the overshoot frequency is ",
         fpc(e_small$tail_frac, 1, signed = FALSE), ". A single small release ",
         "group can therefore look unremarkable on a median-based diagnostic ",
         "while contributing a large upward pull to a pooled estimate. The ",
         "mean overstates the typical group, the median conceals the tail ",
         "entirely, and the frequency is the statistic that says what a reader ",
         "of a real assessment should actually expect to encounter: not that ",
         "every small group is biased, but that some fraction of them are ",
         "badly so. ", e_lever)
} else {
  paste0("Locating an effect this small needs a design that pushes the ",
         "noise-to-signal ratio harder than release-group size can on its ",
         "own. ", e_lever)
}

# Limitations bullet, which has to describe either a resolved effect or a
# bounded null depending on how the experiment came out.
e_limit <- if (e_resolved && e_tail_gap > 0) {
  paste0("**Experiment E resolves a difference, not a curve, and the mean it ",
         "reports is not a bias correction.** The design separates the ",
         "smallest and largest release-group sizes by ",
         fpc(abs(e_tail_gap), 1, signed = FALSE), " in overshoot frequency, ",
         "against a joint Monte Carlo standard error of ",
         fpc(e_tail_gap_mcse, 1, signed = FALSE),
         ", which establishes that group size matters but does not pin down ",
         "the functional form between the two ends. The mean at the smallest ",
         "group size is driven by a small number of extreme replicates and ",
         "carries a large standard error of its own (",
         fpc(e_small$mean_mcse, 1, signed = FALSE), "); ",
         if (e_mean_stable)
           paste0("it is stable to a large widening of the search interval, ",
                  "but it remains a statistic about a tail and should be read ",
                  "as evidence of one rather than as a number to subtract off ",
                  "an assessment. ")
         else
           paste0("it also moves when the search interval is widened, so it ",
                  "is partly a property of where the upper bound on F was ",
                  "placed and should not be quoted as a bias estimate at all. "),
         "The solved F is unbounded above in principle, so any mean of it is ",
         "conditional on a bound imposed by the analyst -- which is a general ",
         "property of the deterministic inversion, not an artefact of this ",
         "simulation. Release-group size also varies total tags alongside ",
         "group size, so precision varies across the design, which is why ",
         "every statistic is reported with its own Monte Carlo standard error.")
} else {
  paste0("**Experiment E is underpowered for the effect it tests.** The ",
         "design resolves a difference of roughly ",
         fpc(e_mde, 1, signed = FALSE), " in overshoot frequency between the ",
         "smallest and largest release-group sizes, and the convexity effect ",
         "at these sample sizes may be smaller than that. It uses a single ",
         "release group rather than a pooled set, and reports a tail ",
         "frequency and a mean alongside the median, all of which give the ",
         "mechanism a better chance of showing than a pooled median would; it ",
         "does not follow that a null result rules the mechanism out. ",
         "Release-group size also varies total tags alongside group size, so ",
         "precision varies across the design, which is why every statistic is ",
         "reported with its own Monte Carlo standard error.")
}

# Checklist item, likewise.
e_check <- if (e_resolved && e_tail_gap > 0) {
  paste0("The default inverts a noisy observation, and that inversion is ",
         "convex in the observation, so small release groups put weight in ",
         "the upper tail of $F$ that the large-sample argument does not ",
         "predict. At ", e_small$N0_e, " tags per group, ",
         fpc(e_small$tail_frac, 1, signed = FALSE), " of release groups ",
         "return an estimate more than ", E_TAIL_MULT, " times the truth with ",
         "the reporting rate correct and the floor inactive, against ",
         fpc(e_large$tail_frac, 1, signed = FALSE), " at ",
         format(e_large$N0_e, big.mark = ","), ". Note that the median at the ",
         "small-group cell ", e_med_phrase_short, ": the cost is a heavy ",
         "right tail across release groups, not a shift every group shares, ",
         "so it will not show up in a diagnostic built on medians. Count the ",
         "releases per group in the `.tag` file and check how much of the ",
         "tagging data sits in groups of a few hundred.")
} else {
  paste0("The default inverts a noisy observation, and that inversion is ",
         "convex in the observation, so small release groups are a candidate ",
         "source of upward bias in $F$ independent of the reporting rate and ",
         "the floor. Experiment E did not resolve such an effect, but it was ",
         "not powered to exclude one of a few percent, so group sizes are ",
         "still worth reporting alongside the other two conditions.")
}
```

`r e_verdict`

`r e_next`

Note that this experiment isolates group size from the survival floor — the
reporting rate is correct, so the raised target is correct on average and the
floor is not the operative mechanism. In a real configuration the two run
together, and small groups make floor engagement more likely as well.

# What the results show

```{r}
#| label: results-inline
#| include: false
r_f0_eq   <- summ_b[case == "true = assumed" & mode == "flag0", max(abs(rel_bias))]
r_f1_eq   <- summ_b[case == "true = assumed" & mode == "flag1", min(rel_bias)]
r_c_bad   <- summ_c[mode == "flag0" & X_assumed == 0.20 & phi == 2, min(med)]

# flag0 vs forward across Experiment B, by phi.
gap_b <- dcast(summ_b[mode %in% c("flag0", "forward")],
               nmix + phi + case ~ mode, value.var = "rel_bias")
gap_b[, gap := abs(flag0 - forward)]
g_lo   <- gap_b[phi == 0.5, max(gap)]
g_lo_o <- gap_b[phi == 0.5 & case != "true > assumed", max(gap)]
g_hi   <- gap_b[which.max(gap)]

# forward_X accuracy across the 27 cells.
fx_b <- summ_b[mode == "forward_X"]
fx_n4 <- sum(abs(fx_b$rel_bias) <= 0.04)
fx_thr <- ceiling(1000 * max(abs(fx_b$rel_bias[abs(fx_b$rel_bias) <=
             sort(abs(fx_b$rel_bias), decreasing = TRUE)[2]]))) / 10
fx_worst <- fx_b[order(-abs(rel_bias))][1:2]

# nmix escalation at phi = 2, true > assumed.
esc <- dcast(summ_b[phi == 2 & case == "true > assumed" &
                      mode %in% c("flag0", "forward", "forward_X")],
             nmix ~ mode, value.var = "rel_bias")[order(nmix)]
```

**1. When the assumed reporting rate is right, `flag0` is unbiased and `flag1`
is not — and this holds across the whole Experiment B configuration space.**
`flag0` recovers $F$ regardless of $\varphi$ and `nmix` (largest absolute median
bias `r fpc(r_f0_eq, 1, signed = FALSE)`), because the deterministic inversion
never needs to know how available tagged fish were. `flag1` asserts $X = 1$
during mixing, which is false for every tagging programme ever run; its bias in
$F$ is downward, meaning biomass biased *upward*, reaching `r fpc(r_f1_eq)` in
the worst cell, and it worsens steeply as either the mixing period lengthens or
tagged fish become more vulnerable. `tag_flags(i,2) = 1` is a robustness choice,
not a correctness fix, and it errs optimistically.

Experiments C and E qualify this heavily. The unbiasedness of `flag0` survives a
reporting rate that is correct only on average rather than group by group, and it
survives clumped reporting *provided the survival floor does not engage*. Where
it does — low assumed reporting rates, high availability — `flag0`'s median bias
reaches `r fpc(r_c_bad)`, because a capped removal is an under-removal and
under-removal is `flag1`'s error. `r if (e_resolved && e_tail_gap > 0) "Experiment E adds a third condition: the result is a large-sample one, and it degrades at realistic release-group sizes." else "Experiment E looked for a third condition -- a small-sample bias from inverting a noisy target -- and did not resolve one, though it was not powered to rule out a small effect. On current evidence the two conditions above are the operative ones."`
The claim that the default is unbiased holds only inside a region of
configuration space, and that region shrinks as assumed reporting rates fall.

**2. The reporting rate, not the flag, is the first-order channel — except at
high availability.** The `forward` estimator handles mixing correctly but keeps
$X$ fixed at the wrong value, so the gap between it and `flag0` measures what the
mixing treatment contributes over and above the reporting-rate error. Across the
low-availability part of the design that gap is small: at $\varphi = 0.5$ it
never exceeds `r fpc(g_lo, 1, signed = FALSE)`, and outside the
`true > assumed` column it never exceeds `r fpc(g_lo_o, 1, signed = FALSE)`. A
wrong reporting rate rescales every predicted return in the *informative* periods
too, not just the mixing ones, and that channel dominates.

The exception matters. The largest gap in the design is
`r fpc(g_hi$gap, 0, signed = FALSE)`, at $\varphi = `r g_hi$phi`$,
`nmix = `r g_hi$nmix``, `r as.character(g_hi$case)` — `r fpc(g_hi$flag0)` for
`flag0` against `r fpc(g_hi$forward)` for `forward`. Where tagged fish are highly
available during a long mixing period, the deterministic removal stops being a
second-order correction and becomes a large error in its own right. So the flag
is not *always* the minor channel; it is minor in the regime the mixing period
was designed for ($\varphi < 1$) and major in the regime that is arguably more
realistic for purse-seine tagging. Experiment C shows the same boundary in a
different coordinate: the gap is negligible where the floor is inactive and
first-order where it is not. Attributing a biomass shift entirely to the flag
will not survive a sensitivity run, but nor will dismissing it without knowing
where in $\varphi$ the fishery sits.

**3. The two flag settings form a one-sided interval and cannot bracket the
truth when the assumed reporting rate is too high.** Because $X_{assumed} < 1$,
`flag0` always removes more tags than `flag1` and always returns the larger
$\hat{F}$; the interval therefore has `flag0` as its upper end. It can only
contain the truth when `flag0` sits above it, which happens only when the true
reporting rate is at or above the assumed value. Across the entire 27-cell
design, bracketing
`r if (brk_lt == 0) "never occurs in any replicate" else paste0("occurs in at most ", fnum(brk_lt, 0), "% of replicates")`
whenever the true rate is below the assumed one. Where bracketing does occur it is either
degenerate (`true = assumed`, where `flag0` is simply unbiased and noise straddles
the truth roughly half the time) or genuine but extremely wide (high $\varphi$,
`true > assumed`, intervals up to `r fnum(w_max, 1)` times $F$).

**Implication for grid design:** running `tag_flags(i,2)` at 0 and 1 as
alternative levels spans an assumption; it does not bound the truth, and the
direction in which it fails to bound depends on the sign of the reporting-rate
error — which is exactly the thing under dispute. If the real uncertainty is in
the reporting rate, that is what belongs on the grid.

**4. Longer mixing periods amplify a reporting-rate error under every estimator
except `forward_X`.** This is a correction to an expectation worth stating
explicitly, because the intuition that "the forward model turns excluded data
into information, so longer mixing should help" is not what the simulation shows.
At $\varphi = 2$ with the rate underestimated, `flag0` runs
`r fpc(esc$flag0[1])` → `r fpc(esc$flag0[nrow(esc)])` as `nmix` goes 2 → 4. But
`forward` degrades too (`r fpc(esc$forward[1])` → `r fpc(esc$forward[nrow(esc)])`
over the same range), because fixing $X$ at the wrong value contaminates the
extra mixing-period observations just as it contaminates the post-mixing ones.
Adding data does not help when the added data are being scored against a
misspecified nuisance parameter.

Only `forward_X`, which lets $X$ move, is flat in `nmix`
(`r fpc(esc$forward_X[1])` → `r fpc(esc$forward_X[nrow(esc)])`). The lesson is
that handling the mixing period as a likelihood is necessary but not sufficient;
the benefit only materialises when the reporting rate is estimable. Any
sensitivity to `tag_flags(i,1)` in a real assessment should be read as partly a
reporting-rate sensitivity in disguise.

**5. Only estimating the reporting rate fixes the misspecification.**
`forward_X` recovers $F$ to within `r fnum(fx_thr, 1)`% in 26 of the 27 cells of
Experiment B — `r fx_n4` of 27 at a 4% threshold — and recovers $\varphi$ at all
three values tested. The two largest residuals are
`r paste(sprintf("%s (nmix = %s, phi = %s, %s)", fpc(fx_worst$rel_bias, 1), fx_worst$nmix, fx_worst$phi, as.character(fx_worst$case)), collapse = " and ")`,
each within `r fnum(max(abs(fx_worst$rel_bias) / fx_worst$mcse), 1)` Monte Carlo
standard errors of zero, against a typical MCSE for this estimator of
`r fpc(median(fx_b$mcse), 1, signed = FALSE)` — `forward_X` is much the noisiest
of the four, so its worst cells are where noise would be expected to show.
The structural reason it works at all is that under
`flag0` and `flag1` the reporting rate deterministically rewrites the tagged
population and the data have no mechanism to object; under the forward
parameterisation the mixing-period returns become evidence about $X$ rather than
an instruction. Note the caveat in the Limitations: this vignette identifies $X$
far more cleanly than MULTIFAN-CL could.

**6. The default's failure mode is real, and it is triggered by low assumed
reporting rates in combination with high availability, not by uncertainty in the
rate.** The floor engages when the realised catch fraction in a mixing period
exceeds $(1-\tau)X_{assumed}$, about `r fnum(1 - CUT - FRINGE, 2)` times the
assumed rate under MULTIFAN-CL defaults — a fifth easier to reach than the
exhaustion condition $C_t/N_t > X_{assumed}$ that the obvious reading of the
manual suggests. At an assumed rate of 0.5 with $\varphi = 1$ that is not reached
in this design; at 0.5 with $\varphi = 2$ it is reached in
`r fpp_range(ro_hi_p2)` of replicates, and at 0.2 with
$\varphi = 2$ in `r fpp_range(ro_lo_hi)`.

Trip-level clumping *amplifies* this but is not required for it. Small release
groups and stochastic recaptures are sufficient on their own: with trips taking
only 1% of a release group — effectively independent reporting — the floor still
engages in `r fnum(ro_trip_lo$pct[1], 0)`% of replicates at
$X_{assumed} = 0.2$, $\varphi = 1$, and `r fnum(ro_fine_p2, 0)`% at
$\varphi = 2$. This matters for how the result is defended: clumping is the
ingredient an unsympathetic reader will call contrived, and the finding does not
depend on it. An assessment that revises its tag-seeding estimates downward moves
itself into this regime without changing anything else.

**7. Under floor engagement, the default degenerates into the alternative.**
Where the floor rarely engages, clumped reporting costs `flag0` precision but not
accuracy — the median stays within
`r fpc(max(abs(c_f0_safe$med)), 0, signed = FALSE)` while the interquartile range
roughly `r if (max(c_f0_safe$iqr) / min(c_f0_safe$iqr) > 2.5) "triples" else "doubles"`.
Where it routinely engages, `flag0` loses accuracy too, and in the same direction
as `flag1`: once `posfun` caps the removal the default cannot remove the number
of tags its own rule demands, so it under-removes and $F$ is biased downward
(median `r fpc(r_c_bad)` at $X_{assumed} = 0.2$, $\varphi = 2$). The practical
consequence is that the two settings are not as different as they look in the
regime where the choice matters most. Neither behaviour would be visible in
standard assessment diagnostics, which is an argument for checking the floor
condition directly rather than inferring it from fit statistics.

**8. `flag1`'s bias is a function of one measurable quantity.** The mixing-period
recapture fraction $\psi$ collapses $\varphi$ and `nmix` onto a single axis, and
the analytic approximation $-(1-X)\psi N_0 / (N_{post} + (1-X)\psi N_0)$ tracks
the simulation closely (correlation `r fnum(d_cor, 3)`). This makes the question
empirical rather than general: compute $\psi$ from the `.tag` file and the
expected downward bias in $F$ follows — a few percent at $\psi = 0.05$, roughly a
third of $F$ at $\psi = 0.3$, more than half at $\psi = 0.5$.

**9. The likelihood-based treatment is not free.** `forward_X` recovers $F$ and
$X$ cleanly in Experiments A and B, where one release group of 10,000 tags
carries the information. In Experiment C's more realistic configuration — eight
groups of 500 — it is the widest of the four estimators in
`r fnum(100 * c_fx_widest, 0)`% of cells and its median wanders over
`r fpc_range(c_fx$med)`. Structural correctness does not substitute for
information: estimating the reporting rate, the availability multiplier and $F$
together needs data that a fragmented tagging programme may not provide. This
tempers the recommendation in point 5, and it is a reason to treat a code change
as a medium-term improvement rather than a fix available to the current
assessment.

`r if (e_resolved && e_tail_gap > 0) paste0("**10. Release-group size is a structural assumption.** Experiment E shows the default's unbiasedness is a large-sample property: inverting a noisy target is convex in the target, so small release groups put weight in the upper tail of F even when the reporting rate is correct and the floor is inactive. At ", e_small$N0_e, " tags per group, ", fpc(e_small$tail_frac, 1, signed = FALSE), " of groups return an estimate more than ", E_TAIL_MULT, " times the truth, against ", fpc(e_large$tail_frac, 1, signed = FALSE), " at ", format(e_large$N0_e, big.mark = ","), ", while the median at the small-group cell ", e_med_phrase_short, ". The failure is a tail, not a shift, which is why it is invisible to the diagnostics an assessment normally reports. Release-group size is not usually treated as an assumption worth stating; on this evidence it is one.") else "**10. Release-group size was tested and did not turn up as a third condition.** The convexity of the deterministic inversion predicts extra weight in the upper tail of F at small release-group sizes, independent of the reporting rate and the floor. Experiment E did not resolve one, using a tail frequency and a mean alongside the median and a single release group so as to give the mechanism the best chance of showing. This is a bounded null rather than a clean negative, but it means the two conditions in point 1 are the ones to check in practice, and release-group size need not be added to them."`

# What to check in an assessment that fits to tags

This is the practical residue of the five experiments, in the order it is worth
working through. It sits here rather than in the executive summary because every
figure it refers to has been produced by the time it renders, so the numbers
below are read from the fitted objects rather than transcribed.

**1. Which setting was used, and whether it was held constant.**
`tag_flags(i,2)` was inert in MULTIFAN-CL until version 2.2.7.6 (July 2025), so
any comparison against an earlier assessment involves a model change rather than
a like-for-like retrospective. "They used the default" describes the behaviour
correctly but not a decision anyone made — the alternative did not exist. A
change of setting between a draft and a final model would move biomass in a
predictable direction and should be documented as a structural choice, not a bug
fix.

**2. The assumed reporting rates, and the direction of any revision.** This is
the first-order channel through most of the design: at $\varphi = 0.5$ the gap
between the deterministic treatment and a correctly specified forward model
never exceeds `r fpc(g_lo, 1, signed = FALSE)`. A downward revision of
tag-seeding estimates raises inferred $F$ and lowers biomass through the
ordinary likelihood, *and* separately pushes the model toward the regime where
the default breaks down. The two effects compound and are easily conflated. The
exception is high availability during a long mixing period, where the flag
becomes a first-order channel in its own right (largest gap in the design
`r fpc(g_hi$gap, 0, signed = FALSE)`, at $\varphi = `r g_hi$phi`$,
`nmix = `r g_hi$nmix``). For the 2026 bigeye assessment the values and the
direction of revision are both documented: SC22-SA-IP-05 gives purse seine
reporting-rate priors with means of 0.496 in region 2, 0.512 in region 3 and
0.528 in region 4, each between 15 and 24 per cent below what the 2023
assessments would have used under the same region and fishery definitions, with
the reduction driven largely by the introduction of double-tag effects. Read
those as penalty distributions rather than fixed values — the model estimates
the rate against them — and note that they cover purse seine fleets only, that
the region 2 penalty was deliberately halved to reflect additional uncertainty,
and that the region 2 prior is not recommended for the Indonesian and Philippine
domestic fisheries.

**3. Whether the survival floor is engaging.** The floor engages when the
realised catch fraction in a mixing period exceeds $(1-\tau)X_{assumed}$, about
`r fnum(1 - CUT - FRINGE, 2)` times the assumed rate under MULTIFAN-CL defaults
— that is `r fnum((1 - CUT - FRINGE) * 0.5, 3)` at an assumed rate of 0.5 and
`r fnum((1 - CUT - FRINGE) * 0.2, 3)` at 0.2, which ordinary fishing mortalities
reach. When it happens, `posfun` silently caps the removal and the default then
**under-removes**, biasing $F$ downward and biomass upward — the same direction
as the alternative it is supposed to improve on. In MULTIFAN-CL the floor is set
by `age_flags(118)` and `(119)`, with a penalty weighted by
`age_flags(117)/1e8`; if `age_flags(117) < 0` the penalty weight is zero and the
rescaling leaves no trace in the objective function at all. Check
`age_flags(117)`, `(118)` and `(119)`, and check whether `age_flags(198)`
(release-group-specific reporting rates) is active, which makes the divisor vary
by group.

**4. The mixing-period recapture fraction $\psi$.** For `tag_flags(i,2) = 1` the
downward bias in $F$ is largely governed by this one measurable quantity: the
proportion of each release group *recaptured* within `tag_flags(i,1)` periods of
release. The `.tag` file records reported returns rather than recaptures, so the
returns have to be raised before dividing:

$$\hat\psi_i \;\approx\; \frac{1}{X} \cdot
  \frac{\sum_{t \le \texttt{tag\_flags}(i,1)} R_{it}}{N_i}.$$

Omitting the $1/X$ returns $X\psi$ rather than $\psi$, which at a reporting rate
near 0.5 halves the diagnosed fraction — and because the bias steepens with
$\psi$, it understates the consequence by more than half again. Then read the
bias off Experiment D or evaluate
$-(1-X)\psi N_0 / (N_{post} + (1-X)\psi N_0)$ directly:
`r fpc_range(unlist(suff_at(0.05)[, .(worst, best)]), 1)` at $\psi = 0.05$;
`r fpc_range(unlist(suff_at(0.30)[, .(worst, best)]), 1)` at $\psi = 0.3$;
`r fpc_range(unlist(suff_top[, .(worst, best)]), 1)` at
$\psi = `r fnum(suff_top_psi, 2)`$. Each range is printed worst-first, and
because a longer mixing period carries the worse bias at a given $\psi$ — the
ordering the Experiment D tripwire guards — the worst end is the longest mixing
length. Take that end where `tag_flags(i,1)` is large. Two caveats:
$\hat\psi$ inherits any error in the reporting rate it is raised by, in the
direction that understates the problem; and a
release-group-weighted mean aggregates over groups whose mixing lengths differ.
This is an afternoon's work against the `.tag` file and it turns a
general argument into a specific one about that assessment's data.

**5. The size of the release groups.** `r e_check`

**6. Whether the flag appears as a grid axis, and how it is described.** Running
both settings spans an assumption; it does not bound the truth. The pair is
structurally one-sided — the default always returns the larger $F$ — so it can
never bracket when the assumed reporting rate is too high, and where it does
bracket the interval reaches `r fnum(w_max, 1)` times the quantity being
estimated. If the real uncertainty is in the reporting rate, that is what
belongs on the grid.

# Guidance on `tag_flags(i,2)`

Neither setting of `tag_flags(i,2)` is correct, and the choice between them
should be made and reported as a conditional one.

Simulation testing shows that the default, `tag_flags(i,2) = 0`, recovers fishing
mortality without appreciable bias when the assumed tag reporting rate is
correct, across all combinations of mixing-period length (2–4 quarters) and
tagged-fish availability ($\varphi$ = 0.5–2) tested in Experiment B. That
robustness is structural: the deterministic inversion solves for whatever
mixing-period fishing mortality reproduces the implied removal, so it does not
require the availability of tagged fish during mixing to be correctly specified.

It is, however, conditional on further requirements, and the claim should not be
extended past the design in which it was demonstrated. Where the realised catch
fraction in a mixing period exceeds roughly four-fifths of the assumed reporting
rate, the raised removal drives the tagged population below the survival floor,
the floor engages, and the default then under-removes — biasing fishing mortality
downward by as much as `r fpc(abs(r_c_bad), 0, signed = FALSE)` in our tests.
This condition is reached routinely at assumed reporting rates around 0.2, and at
0.5 whenever tagged fish are substantially more available during mixing than the
general population. The default's reliability therefore declines precisely as
reporting-rate estimates are revised downward — and they are being revised
downward. The purse seine reporting-rate priors for bigeye in SC22-SA-IP-05 have
means of 0.496 to 0.528 across regions 2 to 4, between 15 and 24 per cent below
the values the 2023 assessments would have used under the same region and
fishery definitions. The 2026 bigeye assessment therefore sits at the boundary
of this condition, not safely inside it, and a further revision of the magnitude
just observed would move it across.
`r if (e_resolved && e_tail_gap > 0) paste0("Separately, the result is a large-sample one: at ", e_small$N0_e, " tags per release group, ", fpc(e_small$tail_frac, 1, signed = FALSE), " of release groups return an estimate of fishing mortality more than ", E_TAIL_MULT, " times the truth even with a correct reporting rate and an inactive floor, while the median at the same cell ", e_med_phrase_short, ". The cost is a heavy right tail across release groups rather than a shift each group shares, so it is invisible to a median-based check and it does not average away as quickly as pooling suggests.") else "Release-group size was tested as a possible third condition and did not emerge as one, though the test does not exclude a small effect."`

The alternative, `tag_flags(i,2) = 1`, assumes complete reporting during the
mixing period. This is not true of any tagging programme, and the resulting bias
is systematic rather than conservative: fishing mortality is underestimated and
biomass correspondingly overestimated, with the error growing as either the
mixing period lengthens or tagged fish become more available. Under plausible
configurations the bias in fishing mortality reached
`r fpc(abs(r_f1_eq), 0, signed = FALSE)`. Its one merit is predictability — the
bias is largely a function of the proportion of each release group recaptured
during the mixing period, which is computable from the `.tag` file in advance
provided the reported returns are raised by the assumed reporting rate first.
The qualifier matters in both directions: the recapture fraction does not
determine the bias entirely, since at a fixed fraction a longer mixing period is
worse by `r fpc(suff_top$spread, 1, signed = FALSE)` at the top of the range
tested; and an analyst who forgets the raising will diagnose half the fraction
and conclude the setting is far cheaper than it is.

On balance the default remains preferable where reporting rates are moderate,
tagged-fish availability during mixing is not elevated, the survival floor is
demonstrably not engaging`r if (e_resolved && e_tail_gap > 0) ", and release groups are large enough for the large-sample argument to apply" else ""`.
`r if (e_resolved && e_tail_gap > 0) "All four conditions" else "All three conditions"`
should be checked and reported rather than assumed. Neither setting protects
against misspecification of the reporting rate itself, which is the larger error
channel in most cases examined;
the two settings do not bracket the truth and should not be used as alternative
levels in a structural uncertainty grid. Where reporting rates are uncertain,
that uncertainty should be represented directly.

The treatment that would resolve the dilemma rather than manage it is to predict
mixing-period returns and score them in the likelihood, with the reporting rate
estimated against its tag-seeding prior. MULTIFAN-CL cannot currently do this —
under both settings the mixing-period predictions are constructed from the
observed returns rather than from the tagged cohort, so nothing is scored as
evidence about that cohort — and it is therefore a request to the MULTIFAN-CL
development team rather than something an assessment can configure. We recommend
it as a medium-term change, with the caveat that the simulation here also shows
it is not free: with many small release groups it was the least precise of the
four estimators tested, under a prior looser than any assessment would impose.

Because both settings are biased and the choice is unavoidable in any model
fitted to tags, we further recommend that a configuration omitting tagging data —
with spatial structure carried by a fleets-as-areas approach — be included in the
structural uncertainty grid. This bounds the influence of the tag data on stock
status without requiring the mixing-period treatment to be resolved first, and it
answers a question of direct management relevance: how much of the assessment
result depends on the tagging programme. This recommendation follows from the
demonstrated deficiencies of both flag settings rather than from any simulation
of a spatial model, which is outside the scope of this vignette.

# Limitations

This is a deliberately stripped-down operating model and it flatters the forward
model in ways a real assessment would not.

- **The number of tags released is known exactly**, and there is no abundance,
  selectivity, movement, or catchability to confound with the reporting rate.
  Identification of $X$ here is far stronger than in MULTIFAN-CL, where $X$
  trades off against $q$ and against absolute abundance. The extent to which
  `forward_X` rescues a bad prior is therefore optimistic, and the prior
  standard deviation (0.4 on the log scale) is loose. Tightening it toward a
  hard tag-seeding constraint moves `forward_X` back toward `forward`.
- **$\varphi$ is a single scalar applied uniformly across the mixing period.**
  In reality availability presumably decays smoothly from release, and varies by
  fishery. A step function is the simplest possible caricature.
- **No spatial structure.** The reason a mixing period exists at all is that
  effort is not randomly distributed relative to release sites; that spatial
  process is represented here only through its effect on $\varphi$.
- **Observation error.** Experiments A, B, D and E use unclumped reporting;
  Experiment C adds trip-level clumping but the likelihood remains Poisson,
  whereas MULTIFAN-CL offers negative binomial and binned options via
  `parest_flags(111)`. Fitting a likelihood matched to the clumping would narrow
  the dispersion penalty seen in Experiment C.
- **The `posfun` analogue is approximate, and its penalty does no work.** The
  smooth floor and quadratic penalty reproduce the qualitative behaviour of
  `do_newton_raphson_for_tags()` — catch capped, survival floored — but it is not
  a transcription of the MULTIFAN-CL code, and the weight is set by hand rather
  than derived from `age_flags(117)`. More importantly, because the mixing target
  depends only on the data and not on any parameter, the penalty is constant with
  respect to the parameter vector and cannot influence $\hat{F}$. That makes this
  vignette a faithful model of the `age_flags(117) < 0` case specifically. A
  configuration with a positive penalty weight might behave differently, and
  nothing here tests that.
- **Clumping is modelled as a single trip size.** Real reporting varies by
  fleet, and a mixture of well-reporting and non-reporting fleets would behave
  differently from a homogeneous trip process with the same mean. At the coarsest
  trip setting the realised number of trips per release group per period falls to
  a handful, so that corner of the design should be read as an extreme rather
  than as a typical fishery.
- **The forward estimators are not tuned for the Experiment C sample size.**
  `forward_X` estimates three parameters from eight groups of 500 tags under a
  loose prior; its poor performance there reflects that configuration rather than
  a defect of the parameterisation. A tighter prior, more release groups, or
  fewer free parameters would all improve it, and this vignette does not locate
  the boundary.
- **Experiment C fixes the mixing length at `nmix = 3`.** Experiment B's claim of
  robustness across mixing lengths is therefore not re-tested under the realistic
  observation model.
- `r e_limit`
- **No spatial or fleets-as-areas configuration is simulated.** The
  recommendation to include a tag-free branch in a structural uncertainty grid
  follows from the demonstrated deficiencies of both flag settings, not from any
  result in this document.
- **$\psi$ is treated as known.** In practice it would be estimated from
  observed recaptures, which are themselves thinned by the reporting rate, so a
  real calculation would need to raise them — reintroducing some of the
  uncertainty the exercise is trying to characterise.

# Suggested extensions

- Replace the Poisson observation model with a negative binomial and estimate the
  dispersion, to see how much of the contrast survives realistic overdispersion.
- Let $\varphi$ decay geometrically with quarters at liberty rather than
  switching off at `nmix`, and estimate the decay rate. This is closer to the
  biology and would show whether `tag_flags(i,1)` needs to be a sharp boundary
  at all.
- Add multiple release cohorts with $\varphi$ grouped by quarter at liberty —
  the structure that makes $\varphi$ identifiable in a real model, and worth
  demonstrating before proposing it to the developers.
- **Sweep the prior standard deviation on $X$ in `forward_X`, and treat this as
  the highest-value outstanding run in this list.** The value used throughout is
  0.4 on the log scale. The penalty parameters in SC22-SA-IP-05 imply
  coefficients of variation on the bigeye purse seine reporting rate of roughly
  0.05 to 0.09 — close to an order of magnitude tighter than the prior imposed
  here. `forward_X` was the least precise estimator tested in this document, and
  that finding is one of the reasons given for treating a likelihood-based
  treatment as a medium-term development request rather than a current option.
  Until the sweep is run it is not possible to say how much of the imprecision
  is intrinsic to the estimator and how much is an artefact of a prior far
  looser than any assessment would impose. The sweep would also locate where the
  ability to revise the reporting rate is lost, which is the other half of the
  trade-off.
- Fit with `nmix` misspecified relative to the truth, since in practice the
  analyst chooses `tag_flags(i,1)` without knowing the real mixing time.
- Add a `forward` variant with $\varphi$ fixed at 1. The current
  `flag0`–`forward` gap conflates two changes — scoring the mixing-period returns
  in the likelihood, and adding a free availability parameter — so it does not
  cleanly isolate the mixing channel.
- Give the survival-floor penalty something to act on, by making the mixing-period
  target depend on an estimated quantity, and check whether a positive
  `age_flags(117)` changes the Experiment C conclusions.
- **Establish what bounds the solved $F$ in MULTIFAN-CL.** In this vignette the
  deterministic inversion is unbounded above and is held in check by an explicit
  search interval, which is why every tail statistic here is reported against a
  boundary-contact diagnostic. A real implementation has its own effective bound —
  through parameter bounds on $F$, through the survival floor, or through the
  Newton solver's own failure behaviour — and which of these binds first
  determines what an extreme release group actually does to an assessment.
  Reading that out of the code would say whether the tail found in Experiment E
  is realised as a large $\hat{F}$, as a floored removal, or as a convergence
  failure the analyst would notice.
- Vary `nmix` within Experiment C, to test whether Experiment B's robustness
  across mixing lengths survives the realistic observation model.
- **Push the noise-to-signal ratio through $X_{assumed}$ as well as through
  release-group size**, to separate the two routes into the same mechanism. A
  lower assumed rate thins $R_t$ and inflates the divisor simultaneously, so it
  attacks the ratio harder than $N_0$ can alone, and it is the axis a real
  assessment moves along when seeding estimates are revised. The complication is
  that the low-$X$ region is also where the survival floor engages, so the design
  would need to hold the floor inactive by construction — a large $N_0$ with a
  low $\varphi$, or the floor disabled outright — to attribute any effect to the
  inversion rather than to the cap. Done properly this would also pin down the
  functional form that Experiment E establishes the existence of but does not
  resolve.
- Raise the replicate count in Experiment E and add intermediate group sizes.
  The present design establishes that the two ends differ but leaves the shape
  between them unresolved, and a tail frequency is an inherently noisy statistic:
  its Monte Carlo error scales as $n^{-1/2}$, so halving the resolvable
  difference from the present `r fpc(e_mde, 1, signed = FALSE)` costs four times
  the replicates. That is affordable here, since the flag modes are
  one-dimensional, and it is what would turn the third condition from a
  qualitative warning into something an analyst could calibrate against their own
  release-group sizes.
